docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The purpose of this individual block diagram is to showcse the hardware architecture, electrical interfaces, and signal flow for the Servo Motor Subsystem of Team's Modular Spider Leg.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
• Power Input: The subsystem receives power from an external 9 V DC supply.

  • Main 5 V Supply: An LM7805 regulator produces a regulated 5 V supply for the PIC development board, OLED display, debug LED, push button, and communication circuitry.

  • Servo 5 V Supply: A second LM7805 provides a separate regulated 5 V rail for the Hitec HS-485HB servo. Separating the servo supply reduces the effect of the servo's high current demand and electrical noise on the microcontroller and OLED.

  • Microcontroller: The PIC18F57Q43 acts as the controller. It receives position commands through UART, generates the PWM control signal for the servo, communicates with the OLED through I²C, and controls the debugging inputs and outputs.

  • Servo Control: The Hitec HS-485HB servo receives a PWM signal from the PIC through RC2. The servo converts the commanded pulse width into the required angular position of the spider leg.

  • OLED Display: The 2.42-inch 128 × 64 OLED connects to the PIC through the I²C interface. RB1 provides SCL and RB2 provides SDA. The display shows the commanded servo position, operating status, and diagnostic information.

  • Team Communication: The subsystem connects to the main hub through the team's standard connector. RF0 is configured as UART RX to receive commands, while RF1 is configured as UART TX to return subsystem status.

  • Debugging Interfaces: The RF4 debug LED provides a visible indication of program operation. The RF7 push button provides a manual test input, while the test points allow important power and signal nodes to be measured during troubleshooting.

docs.title: Design Decision
docs.text:
The subsystem uses a hub and spoke structure because it operates as one part of the team's larger modular spider leg system.

The power section is divided into separate main and servo 5 V rails. The main LM7805 supplies the PIC, OLED, and debugging circuitry, while the second LM7805 supplies the Hitec HS-485HB servo. This separation reduces the possibility of the servo's high current demand and electrical noise interfering with the microcontroller or OLED.

docs.title: Driver PIC 1 (Servo + Display)
docs.text:
This page covers the components for Driver PIC 1: the joint-1 servo and the diagnostic display. Driver 1 receives target positions from the Main Processor PIC, drives the joint, shows leg status on the display, and reports status back.

Selection criteria used for both components

  • Runs on 5V.
  • Has a manufacturer or available datasheet.
  • Uses few pins and easy to integrate.

Hip Joint Servo (Rotary Actuator)

  1. Hitec HS-485HB standard analog servo

    • $28.99/each
    • HS-485HB product page at Amzaon
    • HS-485HB manufacturer datasheet
    Pros Cons Position control is built in: the internal potentiometer holds the commanded angle, so the PIC only outputs one 50 Hz PWM signal and no driver IC is needed. Stall current is 1.0 A at 4.8 V and 1.2 A at 6 V per the datasheet, so the regulator and wiring must be sized for it, and the servo cannot be powered from the PIC's 5V pin. Stall torque of 4.8 kgf·cm at 4.8 V and 6.0 kgf·cm at 6 V in a 45 g package gives the highest torque per gram of the three options. Karbonite (plastic) gears can strip under shock loads such as a leg strike, and metal-gear servos cost more. It runs from the same 4.8–6 V range as the logic, and the manufacturer datasheet lists stall current, idle current, speed, and dimensions, which makes the power budget straightforward. The servo gives no position output, so the Nano cannot confirm that the joint reached the angle. The status sent to the Main Nano is the commanded value, not a measured one.

  2. NEMA 17 bipolar stepper (17HS15-1704S) with DRV8825 stepper driver carrier

    • Motor: $9.98
    • 17HS4023S Stepper motor product page at Amazon
    • 17HS15-1704S full datasheet

    • Driver: $15.95
    • DRV8825 driver product page at Pololu
    • DRV8825 datasheet (Texas Instruments)
    Pros Cons The motor's rated current of about 0.7 A per phase is well under the DRV8825 carrier's roughly 1.5 A limit without a heat sink, so no extra cooling is needed. Holding torque is only about 14 N·cm (roughly 1.4 kgf·cm), about a third of the HS-485HB's 4.8 kgf·cm at 4.8 V, so a gearbox would likely be needed for a hip joint, adding cost, backlash, and mass. The DRV8825 provides up to 1/32 microstepping from a 1.8° step motor, and the PIC only has to output STEP and DIR pulses with no PWM timing constraints. The DRV8825 needs an 8.2–45 V motor supply (the motor is rated for 12 V), so it cannot run from the 5–6 V logic rail and adds a second power rail, regulator, and power budget line. The shaft holds position while the coils are energized with no gear train to strip, and the DRV8825 adds over current protection, thermal shutdown, and an adjustable current limit. It is open loop with no position feedback, so lost steps go undetected and the joint needs a homing switch at power up, and the coils draw current continuously while holding.

Choice: Option 1: Hitec HS-485HB standard servo

Reason: The HS-485HB is the best match for the Driver PIC 1 architecture. Its internal closed loop position control means the PIC only needs one pin, and it runs from a 4.8–6 V supply. The stepper option (Option 2) is the most inexpensive motor, but the DRV8825 needs at least 8.2 V, which forces a second different voltage power rail and regulator, and the 280 g motor is about six times heavier than the servo for similar torque.

Diagnostic Display (leg status)

  1. 2.42 inches 128x64 IIC I2C OLED Display Module (Amazon)

    • Price: $15.59
    • 2.42 Inches I2C OLED Display Module on Amazon
    • Oled Display Datasheet
    Pros Cons Large 2.42-inch, 128×64 display provides clear text and enough space for angles, status, and fault messages. The display controller requires more code to run. Uses only four I²C connections: VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL. It is larger and more expensive than common 0.96-inch OLED modules. Supports 3–5 V power and provides bright, high contrast graphics without a backlight. Static images displayed for long periods can cause pixel dimming or burn in.

  2. Adafruit Standard 16×2 character LCD

    • Price: $9.95
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 (ADA181) product page
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 Display Code Datasheet
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 Display Wiring Datasheet
    Pros Cons Adafruit provides a datasheet with pin locations and the HD44780 command set datasheet. It is text-only (16 characters × 2 rows), so it cannot show graphics or a compact status layout. The single-row 0.1" header suits breadboards and through-hole boards. It needs multiple digital lines in 4-bit mode (versus two for an I2C OLED). Adding the I2C backpack would reduce the pins but add cost and put it on the I2C bus. The Liquid Crystal is easy to program with well documented user guides, also it avoids the OLED frame buffer issue. A contrast potentiometer and backlight resistor are needed, and the backlight draws current continuously. The blue LED backlight can be dimmed with a resistor or PWM and uses much less power than backlights. The module is physically larger than the OLED.

Choice: Option 1: 2.42 inches 128x64 IIC I2C OLED Display Module

Reason: The OLED can show multiple lines of leg status (commanded angle, measured status, fault flags) and simple graphics, which the 16×2 LCD cannot. It needs only two signal pins, whereas the LCD needs six or more

Pin Table (Potential Pin Connection Plan, Driver PIC 1)

PIC pin Function Connects to RC2 7 Servo PWM output RB2 9 I2C SDA RB1 10 I2C SCL RC4 11 Spare GPIO RC5 12 Spare GPIO RF0 25 UART TX RF1 26 UART RX RF4 34 Debug LED output RF7 37 Debug push-button input VTG 51 Board power input

Peripheral Connector Wiring

Connector Pin Connection J2 Servo 1 Servo PWM signal from RC2 through R1 J2 Servo 2 +5V_SERVO from JP1 J2 Servo 3 Earth J3 OLED 1 Earth J3 OLED 2 Main +5 V J3 OLED 3 I2C SCL from RB1 J3 OLED 4 I2C SDA from RB2 J5 Expansion 1 Earth J5 Expansion 2 RC5 J5 Expansion 3 RC4 J5 Expansion 4 Main +5 V

The HS-485HB servo is powered by a separate LM7805 regulator. Jumper-1 allows the servo supply to be disconnected during testing. The OLED and PIC development board use the main regulated +5 V supply. All other pins have a common Earth connection.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: The HS-485HB worst case stall current is 1,200 mA. With a 25% safety margin, the servo rail requires 1,500 mA, equal to the assumed LM7805 maximum rating.
